choices: In the cafeteria
At the main gate
In Gym 2
In each office
items.explanation: 「昼食を第二体育館で配ります」: lunch is handed out in Gym 2 because the cafeteria (食堂) is under construction.

items.stem: What is true about lunch time today?
choices: It is the same as usual
It starts earlier than usual
It is shorter than usual
It is cancelled
items.explanation: 「時間はいつもと同じ、十一時半から一時まで」: the time is the same as always, 11:30 to 1:00. Only the place changes.

items.stem: What should people do with the lunch boxes after eating?
choices: Wash them and keep them
Throw them in the trash
Take them back to their office
Return them at the gym entrance
items.explanation: 「お弁当の箱は、食べたあと、体育館の入口に返してください」: return the boxes at the gym entrance. Washing, throwing away, or taking them to the office are not mentioned.

items.stem: Where is the post office?
choices: Across from the station
Next to the bank
Behind the hospital
Next to a convenience store
items.explanation: The man says 「銀行の隣にありますよ」, next to the bank. No station, hospital, or convenience store is mentioned.

items.stem: How should the woman get there?
choices: Go straight and turn left at the second light
Turn right at the first traffic light
Go straight, then right at the second light
Go straight past the bank and turn left
items.explanation: 「まっすぐ行って、二つ目の信号を右に曲がってください」: go straight and turn right at the second light; the woman repeats 「二つ目の信号を右ですね」.

items.stem: About how long does it take on foot?
choices: Five minutes
Two minutes
Ten minutes
Fifteen minutes
items.explanation: To 「歩いて何分ぐらいですか」 the man answers 「五分ぐらいです」, about five minutes. "Two" is the number of traffic lights, not minutes.

items.stem: What does the woman ask for?
choices: The same jacket at a cheaper price
A refund for a jacket she bought
A different style of jacket
This jacket in a larger size
items.explanation: 「このジャケットの、もう少し大きいサイズはありますか」: she wants this jacket in a slightly bigger size. Price, refunds, and other styles are not discussed.

items.stem: Which color does she choose?
choices: Black
Navy blue
Light gray
White
items.explanation: The clerk offers black and navy (黒と紺), and she says 「紺をお願いします」, navy. Light gray and white are not offered.

items.stem: What will the woman probably do next?
choices: Try the jacket on
Pay and leave immediately
Go to another store
Ask for a smaller size
items.explanation: She asks 「試着してもいいですか」 and the clerk points to the fitting room (試着室), so she will try it on. Nothing suggests leaving, going elsewhere, or wanting a smaller size.

items.stem: When will they meet?
choices: Monday at 10:00
Tuesday afternoon
Wednesday afternoon
Wednesday at 10:00 a.m.
items.explanation: Sato suggests 「水曜日の午前十時」 and Kimura agrees. Monday is out because of his trip, and Sato has a meeting Tuesday afternoon.

items.stem: Why can't Kimura meet on Monday?
choices: He has a meeting
He is on a business trip
He is on vacation
The room is already booked
items.explanation: 「月曜日は出張なので」: he is on a business trip Monday. The meeting on Tuesday afternoon is Sato's, not his.

items.stem: What will Sato do after the conversation?
choices: Cancel her Tuesday meeting
Call Kimura on Monday
Reserve the meeting room
Send the agenda to the team
items.explanation: She says 「部屋を予約しておきます」, she will book the room. She does not cancel anything, and calls or agendas are not mentioned.

items.stem: Why is Yuki calling?
choices: To say the restaurant is closed on Sundays
To cancel Saturday lunch and suggest Sunday
To invite the listener to lunch at her office
To move the lunch to a cheaper restaurant
items.explanation: She says she can't come on Saturday because work came up (急に仕事が入って) and asks 「日曜日のお昼はどう？」. She says the restaurant seems to be open on Sunday (やってるみたい), so the first choice is the opposite of what she says.

items.stem: What does Yuki ask the listener to do?
choices: Call the restaurant
Book a table for Saturday
Send her a message later
Meet her at the station at noon
items.explanation: 「あとでメッセージちょうだい」 means "send me a message later." She does not ask the listener to call or book anything, and no meeting is fixed yet.

items.stem: Why did the embassy leave this message?
choices: The passport is ready to be picked up
The passport application was rejected
An interview is required
The consular office is moving
items.explanation: 「パスポートの準備ができました」 and 「受け取りに来てください」: the passport is ready and the listener should come to collect it. Rejection, interviews, and moving are not mentioned.

items.stem: What must the listener bring?
choices: Two passport photos and the processing fee
Their old passport only
The application receipt and ID
A letter from their employer
items.explanation: 「申請の控えと身分証明書をお持ちください」: bring the application copy/receipt (控え) and ID. Photos, fees, old passports, and letters are not mentioned.

items.stem: When can the passport be collected?
choices: Any weekday or weekend until 9:00 p.m.
Weekends only, from 9:00 a.m.
Weekdays after 4:00 p.m.
Weekdays, 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.
items.explanation: 「平日の午前九時から午後四時までに」: on weekdays between 9 a.m. and 4 p.m. Weekends and evenings are outside those hours.

items.stem: What is the main point of the announcement?
choices: The drill has moved to a new location
Tomorrow's drill is postponed to Thursday
The drill is cancelled because of rain
All duty shifts on Thursday are cancelled
items.explanation: 「明日予定していた防災訓練は…木曜日に延期します」: the drill is postponed to Thursday. The place stays the same (場所は変わりません); it is postponed, not cancelled; and duty shifts continue.

items.stem: Who does not have to take part in the drill?
choices: New members
Headquarters staff
Members who were absent this week
People on duty on Thursday
items.explanation: 「木曜日に当直の人は、訓練に参加しなくてもかまいません」: those on duty Thursday may skip it. No other group is excused.

items.stem: Where and when should members gather?
choices: At 8:00 a.m. in the square in front of headquarters
At 8:00 a.m. in the general affairs office
At 10:00 a.m. in the square in front of headquarters
At 8:00 p.m. at the main gate
items.explanation: 「午前八時に、本部前の広場に集まってください」: 8 a.m., the square in front of headquarters. The general affairs office (総務) is only where to ask about duty swaps.

items.stem: What will happen to the City Hall service counters tomorrow?
choices: They will be closed all day tomorrow
They will stay open until 8:00 p.m. instead
They will open but close at 3:00 p.m.
They will offer online services only
items.explanation: 「市役所の窓口は開いていますが、午後三時で閉めます」: the counters are open but close at 3 p.m. It is the libraries and pools that close all day.

items.stem: Which facilities will be closed all day tomorrow?
choices: Libraries and city pools
Hospitals and clinics
Train stations
Supermarkets
items.explanation: 「すべての図書館と市民プールを休館とします」: all libraries and city pools close; schools also close. Hospitals, stations, and shops are not mentioned.

items.stem: What does the city ask residents to do?
choices: Go to the nearest evacuation shelter now
Call City Hall before 3:00 p.m. today
Pick up their children from school early
Avoid unnecessary outings; check the city website
items.explanation: 「最新の情報は、市のホームページでご確認ください」 and 「不要な外出は…控えてください」: check the website and avoid unnecessary outings. No evacuation or phone calls are requested.

items.stem: What must visitors do when they enter the building?
choices: Sign a visitor form on the second floor
Show ID at reception and get a pass
Wait at the entrance for an escort
Leave their phones at the front desk
items.explanation: 「一階の受付で身分証明書を提示し、入館証をお受け取りください」: show ID at the first-floor reception and receive a pass. No forms, escorts, or phone rules are mentioned.

items.stem: What should visitors do with large bags?
choices: Carry them with them at all times inside
Have them searched at the gate
Leave them in lockers by reception
Leave them locked in their car
items.explanation: 「大きな荷物は、受付の横のロッカーに預けていただきます」: large bags go in the lockers beside reception. What must be worn at all times is the pass, not the bags.

items.stem: In this announcement, 「首から下げてください」 tells visitors to:
choices: wear the pass hanging around their neck
put the pass in a pocket
show the pass only when asked
hand the pass to a guard
items.explanation: 首から下げる means to hang something from the neck, so visitors must wear the pass visibly on a lanyard at all times (常に) inside the building.

items.stem: What does Hayashi like about her new apartment?
choices: It is close to the station
It is cheaper than before
It is on a different train line
It is spacious and quiet
items.explanation: 「広くて静かなので気に入っています」: she likes it because it is roomy and quiet. It is farther from the station, the train line is the same, and rent is not mentioned.

items.stem: How does Hayashi get to the station now?
choices: She walks there in about five minutes
She cycles for about ten minutes
She drives her own car
Her coworker gives her a ride
items.explanation: 「駅まで自転車で十分ぐらいかかる」: about ten minutes by bicycle. Walking five minutes was at her old place.

items.stem: What will Hayashi probably do on rainy days?
choices: Take the bus to the station
Work from home
Take a taxi to the office
Ride her bicycle as usual
items.explanation: She says 「雨の日は、バスに乗ろうと思っています」, she plans to take the bus. Working from home, taxis, and cycling in the rain are not her plan.

items.stem: What is the man's problem?
choices: A high fever that started yesterday
A stomachache for the past three days
A three-day cough and a slight fever
A sore throat but no fever at all
items.explanation: 「三日前から、せきが止まらなくて。熱も少しあります」: he has had a cough for three days and a slight fever. The fever is slight, not high, and there is no stomachache.

items.stem: About how long will he have to wait?
choices: Four minutes
Fifteen minutes
One hour
Thirty minutes
items.explanation: 「三十分ほどお待ちいただくと思います」: about thirty minutes. "Four" is the number of people waiting.

items.stem: What can be inferred about the man?
choices: He has never been to this clinic before
He forgot his insurance card
He works in the building next door
He has already filled in the form
items.explanation: 「こちらは初めてなんですが」 shows it is his first visit, which is why he is given the questionnaire (問診票) to fill in. He hands over his insurance card, so he did not forget it.

items.stem: What do the two people decide?
choices: To drive to the hot spring
To go by train
To cancel the trip
To take a long-distance bus
items.explanation: The man concludes 「じゃあ、電車にしよう」, let's take the train. The inn's bus only runs between the station and the inn.

items.stem: What concern does the man raise about going by car?
choices: Parking at the inn is very expensive
He does not have a driver's license
Saturday morning traffic is heavy
The car is too small for their luggage
items.explanation: 「土曜日の朝は道が混むからなあ」: roads get crowded Saturday morning. He actually says the car is easier for luggage, so the last choice is the opposite.

items.stem: How will they get from the station to the inn?
choices: By taxi from the station
On foot
By rental car from the station
By the inn's bus
items.explanation: 「旅館のバスが、駅まで迎えに来てくれる」: the inn's bus will pick them up at the station.

items.stem: Why is Mr. Okawa calling?
choices: To ask about moving out
To arrange a repair visit
To collect the rent
To apologize for a late delivery
items.explanation: He says a repair company (修理の業者) will visit tomorrow about the problem the tenant reported. Moving, rent, and deliveries are not mentioned.

items.stem: What is the problem?
choices: The toilet in the bathroom is blocked
The water heater makes a loud noise
The bath has no hot water
The front door lock is broken
items.explanation: 「お風呂のお湯が出ない件」: the bath has no hot water. The toilet, the water heater noise, and the door lock are not mentioned.

items.stem: What should the listener do if the time is not convenient?
choices: Call by 6:00 today
Call tomorrow at 1:00
Visit the office tomorrow
Leave the key with a neighbor
items.explanation: 「ご都合が悪い場合は、今日の六時までにお電話ください」: if it's inconvenient, call by six today. 1:00–3:00 tomorrow is the visit window, not a time to call.

items.stem: What is the main purpose of the briefing?
choices: To announce that an SDF medical team will be sent to an earthquake zone.
To warn citizens not to travel to the Republic of Minato because of aftershocks.
To explain why the government decided not to send personnel abroad this time.
To report the results of a relief mission that has just ended.
items.explanation: The spokesperson announces the decision to dispatch about eighty SDF medical personnel as an international disaster relief team. The team has not yet left (it departs the day after tomorrow), so it is neither a refusal nor a report on a finished mission, and no travel warning is issued.

items.stem: How long is the team currently expected to operate?
choices: At least two months.
Until the aftershocks stop.
About one month.
About one week.
items.explanation: The spokesperson says the activity period is planned at 一か月程度 for now. Aftershocks are mentioned only as a safety concern, not as the end point of the mission, and neither one week nor two months is mentioned.

items.stem: What does the spokesperson suggest about the risks of the mission?
choices: The main danger is armed groups attacking relief workers.
The team will avoid contact with local authorities for security reasons.
Public order is poor, so the team will be guarded by armed troops from the host country.
Public order seems fairly stable, but continuing aftershocks are a safety concern.
items.explanation: He says security is 比較的安定 but that aftershocks continue, so the team will put members' safety first. He does not call public order poor, and he mentions neither armed groups nor armed guards. He also says the team will stay in close contact with the local government and UN agencies, the opposite of avoiding them.

items.stem: What is the main news in this broadcast?
choices: Landslides have cut off mountain villages, and the governor has asked the Self-Defense Forces for help.
The rain has stopped, so the prefecture is lifting its evacuation calls and reopening the whole expressway.
The expressway has fully reopened, and supplies are now being trucked into the villages that were cut off.
Several villagers were seriously injured in landslides, and the governor has asked other prefectures for rescue teams.
items.explanation: The report says three villages are isolated by landslides and the governor requested a disaster dispatch from the Ground Self-Defense Force. No injuries have been reported so far and the request went to the SDF, not other prefectures; the rain is expected to continue into tonight; and part of the expressway is still closed, so it has not reopened.

items.stem: According to the broadcast, what will the Self-Defense Forces do?
choices: Carry food and water by helicopter and work on restoring roads.
Close the expressway to ordinary traffic.
Search the river for missing people.
Move all residents of the prefecture out by bus.
items.explanation: The SDF will deliver food and water by helicopter (ヘリコプターを使って食料や水を運ぶ) and work on road repairs (道路の復旧作業). Nothing is said about moving the whole prefecture's population, searching a river for missing people, or closing the expressway; the closures are simply reported as continuing.

items.stem: What are people who live near rivers or cliffs asked to do?
choices: Stay at home until the rain stops tonight.
Evacuate while it is still light.
Contact the Self-Defense Forces to request a helicopter.
Avoid the expressway tomorrow morning.
items.explanation: The prefecture asks them to evacuate 明るいうちに, 'while it is still light'. Staying home is the opposite of the request, residents are not told to contact the SDF themselves, and the expressway closure is a separate piece of information, not an instruction to these residents.

items.stem: What is the main point of the news item?
choices: A water utility's control system was attacked, but the water supply was not affected.
Tap water in the city was unsafe to drink for a day after a cyberattack on the purification plant.
Police have arrested the people who attacked the water utility's computer system.
The city has decided to stop using computers at its water plants permanently.
items.explanation: The utility reports unauthorized access that froze some screens, but staff switched to manual operation and there was no effect on supply or water quality. Water safety was not affected, the police are still investigating (no arrests), and the disconnection from the internet is only しばらくの間, 'for the time being'.

items.stem: How did the utility keep operating after the attack?
choices: It restored the system from a backup within an hour.
It shut down the plant until the investigation ended.
It borrowed equipment from a neighboring city.
Staff switched to manual operation.
items.explanation: 職員がすぐに手動での運転に切り替えた: staff immediately switched to manual operation. Backups, borrowed equipment, and a shutdown are not mentioned, and a shutdown would contradict the report that supply was unaffected.

items.stem: What will the utility do for the time being?
choices: Stop supplying water at night.
Hand over plant operations to a private company.
Ask residents to boil their water.
Operate the system disconnected from the internet.
items.explanation: The utility says it will run the system cut off from the internet for a while. Since water quality was unaffected there is no boil-water request, supply continues, and no outside operator is mentioned; a national expert agency is only helping analyze the cause.

items.stem: When will the meeting most likely be held?
choices: Wednesday morning.
Thursday from 2 to 4 p.m.
Wednesday afternoon, starting at 2 p.m.
Tuesday, as originally planned.
items.explanation: The other side asked to move the Tuesday meeting to Wednesday afternoon; Kimura is free from 2 p.m. and Sato has provisionally booked Room 3 from 2 to 4. Tuesday was the original date being changed, and neither Wednesday morning nor Thursday is mentioned.

items.stem: What has to be done by noon on the day before the meeting?
choices: Apply for building passes for the visitors.
Send the meeting documents to the other agencies.
Collect the documents from the last meeting.
Book a larger conference room.
items.explanation: Sato says the 入館証 (building pass) application is due by noon the day before. Documents will not be sent in advance, a room has already been booked, and collecting documents refers to after this meeting, not a prior one.

items.stem: Why will the materials not be sent in advance?
choices: There are too many visitors to send copies to everyone.
The materials are not finished yet.
Some of the content is confidential.
The visitors asked for paper copies only.
items.explanation: Sato explains that some parts involve classified matters (機密に関わる部分), so copies will be handed out in the room and collected afterwards. Nothing suggests the materials are unfinished or that the visitors asked for paper, and six visitors is not described as too many.

items.stem: Where do participants gather first?
choices: At the community center in the afternoon.
At the neighborhood association president's house.
At the community center at 9 a.m.
At the elementary school gym at 9 a.m.
items.explanation: Yamaguchi says they gather at the 公民館 (community center) at nine in the morning. The gym is where they walk to afterwards, the president is only someone to call, and the time is morning, not afternoon.

items.stem: What will happen this year if it rains?
choices: The drill will be held only inside the gym.
The drill will be canceled, as it was last year.
Only the fire extinguisher practice will take place.
The drill will be moved to the following Sunday.
items.explanation: Because last year's drill was rained out, this year it will be held only inside the gym if it rains. Cancellation was last year's outcome, and postponement or holding only extinguisher practice is not mentioned.

items.stem: What will Mr. Nakajima most likely do tonight?
choices: Practice using a fire extinguisher at home.
Call the association president about a ride for his mother.
Tell his mother she cannot join the drill.
Ask Ms. Yamaguchi to drive his mother to the gym on Sunday morning.
items.explanation: Yamaguchi says the association will drive people who cannot walk far if they contact the president by the day before; Nakajima replies that he will call tonight. He wants his mother to attend, and the ride comes from the association's car, not from Yamaguchi.

items.stem: What is the interview mainly about?
choices: A plan to replace rescue workers with automated systems.
How climbers can avoid getting lost in winter.
Why a fire department stopped using drones after one crashed during a winter rescue.
How a fire department's use of drones has changed mountain rescue.
items.explanation: The chief describes introducing drones a year and a half ago, the shorter search times, and their limits. The department still uses drones and no crash is mentioned; he gives no advice to climbers; and he says people are still needed in the end (最後は人の力が必要), so replacing rescuers is not the plan.

items.stem: What happened last winter?
choices: Rescuers walked for hours through the snow before they found a missing climber.
A lost climber was found forty minutes after the emergency call.
The department first introduced drones.
A drone crashed in strong winds.
items.explanation: Last winter a climber who had lost the way was found 通報からわずか四十分. No crash is mentioned; walking for hours describes the situation before drones; and drones were introduced last spring, not winter.

items.stem: What is the department concentrating on now?
choices: Training more personnel to fly the drones.
Buying drones that can fly in heavy snow.
Teaching climbers to use thermal cameras.
Reducing the number of rescue workers.
items.explanation: The chief says they are focusing on training to increase the number of members who can operate drones. He mentions snow only as a condition in which drones cannot fly, says human effort remains essential, and says nothing about training climbers.

items.stem: Why did the farm start employing workers from abroad?
choices: The government required farms to hire foreign workers.
Young people had left the area, so there were not enough hands at harvest time.
Local workers demanded higher wages.
The farm expanded so that it could export strawberries to Vietnam and other countries.
items.explanation: Ishii says young people moved to the cities, leaving the farm short of workers at harvest. Exports, wage demands and government requirements are never mentioned.

items.stem: What helped with the language barrier?
choices: Hiring workers who already spoke Japanese.
An interpreter provided by the city.
Instructions with photos showing each step of the work.
Japanese classes paid for by the farm.
items.explanation: She turned the work procedures into manuals with photos (写真付きの説明書), which the workers found much easier. No interpreter or paid classes are mentioned, and the initial difficulty shows the workers did not already speak Japanese well.

items.stem: Why does Ms. Ishii want to build the dormitory together with neighboring farms?
choices: It would cost too much for a single farm.
The city pays only for shared buildings.
The neighbors own the land where it will be built.
The workers asked to live with workers from other farms.
items.explanation: She says one farm alone could not bear the cost (一つの農家だけでは、費用が大きすぎます). Land ownership, workers' requests and city subsidies are not mentioned.

items.stem: Why did the training end later than planned?
choices: The U.S. unit changed its schedule at short notice.
Residents phoned to complain while it was underway.
The Friday session was moved forward to that night.
One of the vehicles broke down during the drill.
items.explanation: Nakamura explains 「途中で車両が1台故障しまして」, so the last unit left around 10:30. No U.S. change or mid-drill complaints are mentioned; the call came the next morning, and Friday's session is still scheduled for Friday.

items.stem: What bothered the residents most?
choices: The loudness of the vehicles passing their homes
The bright lights used during the night movement
Not knowing when the noise would finally stop
Not being told in advance that there was a drill
items.explanation: Sato relays that 「音そのものよりも、いつ終わるのか分からなかったのが不安だった」. That explicitly puts the noise itself second; lights and lack of advance notice are not mentioned.

items.stem: What will the base do from now on?
choices: Finish all night training by 8 p.m. from now on
Phone the town's duty staff if the finish looks 30+ minutes late
Stop holding night drills near the southern district
Deliver a written notice to every household in the south district in advance
items.explanation: Nakamura promises 「終了が30分以上遅れる見込みになった時点で、役場の当直にお電話する」. The 8 p.m. finish applies only to this Friday, night drills are not stopped, and his extra step is a personal visit to the association head, not letters to households.

items.stem: Why is the town without running water?
choices: Its water treatment plant was damaged by a landslide.
The water pipes froze and burst during the storm.
The town hall ordered water shut off as a precaution.
The roads to the mountain reservoir are all closed.
items.explanation: The reporter says 「浄水場が土砂で壊れたため」 about 1,200 households have no water. Frozen pipes and a precautionary shutoff are not mentioned; closed roads explain why tankers cannot reach the mountain side, not the outage.

items.stem: What is being considered for the mountain-side districts?
choices: Flying water in by helicopter from tomorrow
Building a temporary road for the tankers
Moving residents to the central community hall
Extending the hours of supply to 9 p.m.
items.explanation: The report ends 「ヘリコプターで水を運ぶことも検討している」 because tankers cannot get in. No new road, relocation or longer hours are mentioned; supply runs 7 a.m. to 6 p.m.

items.stem: What is the news story mainly about?
choices: Japan and the Toyo Federation have signed a new defense treaty.
A joint exercise was canceled after a neighboring country protested that it would raise tension.
A ship went missing during a joint exercise.
A first joint exercise has begun, and a neighboring country has objected.
items.explanation: The exercise began today and Hokuryo's foreign ministry expressed concern that it raises regional tension. The protest did not lead to a cancellation, no treaty is mentioned, and 遭難した船の捜索 describes what is being practiced, not a real missing ship.

items.stem: What does the exercise mainly involve?
choices: Live-fire missile tests.
Search and rescue, and communication procedures.
Landing troops on a remote island.
Blocking foreign ships from national waters.
items.explanation: The anchor lists searching for and rescuing ships in distress and communication procedures, and Mori calls these basic areas. None of the other activities is mentioned.

items.stem: Why does Ms. Mori think Hokuryo's reaction was predictable?
choices: The exercise is taking place in waters that Hokuryo claims as its own, near its naval base.
Hokuryo distrusts closer Japan–Toyo Federation ties, whatever the exercise involves.
Hokuryo had been invited to take part but refused.
Japan gave Hokuryo no explanation of the exercise.
items.explanation: She says Hokuryo is wary of the deepening cooperation itself (協力が深まること自体を警戒), so a reaction was expected regardless of content. Disputed waters and an invitation are never mentioned, and she says the government did explain that the exercise targets no specific country.

items.stem: What does Ms. Mori say is important going forward?
choices: Keep explaining its purpose and keep a defense dialogue channel with Hokuryo open.
End cooperation with the Toyo Federation.
Scale down future exercises so that they no longer provoke Hokuryo or other neighbors.
Invite Hokuryo's navy to the next exercise.
items.explanation: She stresses continued careful explanation and maintaining a dialogue channel between defense authorities to prevent accidental clashes. She suggests neither reducing exercises, inviting Hokuryo, nor ending cooperation.

items.stem: What is the main point of the report?
choices: The talks broke down completely, and Japan announced it would stop negotiating.
The talks ended without a deal, but both sides agreed to a joint survey.
Japan agreed to cut its catch by thirty percent.
The two countries signed a new fishing agreement.
items.explanation: No agreement was reached, but the reporter stresses it was not a complete breakdown because both sides agreed on a joint stock survey next month. No agreement was signed, Japan did not walk away, and the thirty percent cut was Nishiumi's demand, not something Japan accepted.

items.stem: What did Nishiumi demand?
choices: A survey carried out only by its own experts.
The same catch as last year.
That Japanese boats leave the overlapping waters entirely.
A thirty percent cut in the total catch.
items.explanation: 西海国側は…全体の量を三割減らすよう主張しました. The same catch as last year is Japan's position, withdrawal from the waters is not mentioned, and the survey will be conducted jointly.

items.stem: As the anchor uses it, 物別れに終わった most nearly means:
choices: ended in a compromise
ended without the two sides reaching agreement
ended earlier than scheduled
ended with both sides satisfied
items.explanation: 物別れ means talks break off with the parties still apart. The anchor uses it right after hearing that no agreement was reached; a compromise or mutual satisfaction would be the opposite, and timing is not what the word describes.

items.stem: Why is the government likely to face a difficult situation?
choices: Nishiumi has threatened to seize Japanese boats that fish in the overlapping waters.
Experts disagree on whether stocks are declining.
The joint survey will be too expensive.
Fishers are anxious that no decision may come before the fishing season starts.
items.explanation: The reporter links the 'difficult steering' to fishers' anxiety that no conclusion will come before the season. Survey costs, threats of seizure and expert disagreement are not mentioned.

items.stem: What are the two council members discussing?
choices: Whether to raise taxes to build a new port.
How best to protect a coastal district from tsunamis.
How to attract young people to fishing.
Whether to close the district's fishing port.
items.explanation: They debate raising the seawall versus supporting relocation to higher ground, both as tsunami protection. Neither proposes closing the port, recruitment and taxes are not discussed, and no new port is planned.

items.stem: What does Ms. Aoki propose?
choices: Helping residents move their homes to higher ground.
Raising the seawall as quickly as possible.
Requiring every resident to relocate.
Moving the fishing port and the fishers' homes to another district.
items.explanation: She says supporting relocation of homes to high ground (高台への移転を支援) protects lives more reliably. She opposes the seawall plan, says residents could still commute to the existing port rather than moving it, and explicitly says she is not saying everyone should be moved.

items.stem: What is Mr. Fujiwara's concern about relocation?
choices: It could undermine the local fishing industry and be hard on older fishers.
It would take more than ten years to complete.
It would cost more than raising the seawall.
People on high ground would lose all access to the port and have to give up fishing.
items.explanation: He fears the local industry could collapse and that older fishers would struggle with the daily climb. Cost is Aoki's argument about doing both measures; he says commuting uphill is hard, not impossible; and the ten-year figure refers to the seawall.

items.stem: How would you describe Ms. Aoki's final remark?
choices: She pushes back, warning that doing both would raise costs further.
She admits her own plan is too expensive.
She changes the subject to the fishing industry.
She accepts Mr. Fujiwara's compromise without reservation.
items.explanation: Responding to his 'do both' idea, she objects that costs would swell and calls for clear priorities. That is disagreement, not acceptance; the cost concern is about his proposal, not hers; and she stays on topic.

items.stem: What is the main topic of the discussion?
choices: Whether language teachers should be replaced by AI tutors that can translate in real time.
How to train professional interpreters.
Whether schools still need in-depth language teaching now that translation apps are good.
Which translation app is the most accurate.
items.explanation: Nishida suggests shifting grammar-teaching time to other subjects because apps are now accurate; Matsumoto argues basics are still needed. No specific apps are compared, replacing teachers is not raised, and Matsumoto says not everyone needs to become an interpreter.

items.stem: On what point do the two speakers agree?
choices: Everyone should aim to become an interpreter.
Grammar should be removed from the curriculum.
Not every student needs to reach the same level.
Translation apps are still unreliable for travel.
items.explanation: Nishida says it is unnecessary to demand the same level from everyone, and Matsumoto answers その点は私も同じ意見です. She does not agree to removing grammar, both accept apps work for travel, and she says not everyone needs to aim to be an interpreter.

items.stem: Why does Ms. Matsumoto think basic language skills are still necessary?
choices: Exams require translating without apps.
Translation apps are too expensive for most students, and schools cannot provide them.
Without them, people cannot judge whether a machine translation is correct.
Machines cannot handle simple travel phrases.
items.explanation: She warns that relying entirely on machines means the ability to judge a translation's accuracy will not develop. Price and exams are not mentioned, and both speakers accept that apps handle travel conversations.

items.stem: Ms. Matsumoto's attitude toward translation technology is best described as:
choices: She is enthusiastic and wants it in every class.
She rejects it as harmful.
She is indifferent to it.
She finds it useful but warns against relying on it completely.
items.explanation: She calls it 便利 (convenient) and wants students to master it as a tool, but cautions against 任せきり (leaving everything to it). That is qualified approval, not rejection, enthusiasm or indifference.

items.stem: What is Mr. Ono's main point?
choices: Remote work has made no real difference to regional areas, as the population figures show.
Companies should stop requiring employees to come to the office.
Remote work has helped regional areas in ways population figures miss.
Local governments should focus only on attracting permanent residents.
items.explanation: Ono argues that although relocation numbers are disappointing, dual-residence people are increasing and contributing locally, so judging only by population misses real change. He rejects the idea that the effect was minimal and warns against reading only the population figures, never criticizes office attendance rules, and says local governments should not focus only on new residents.

items.stem: According to Mr. Ono, why has moving fully to the countryside become difficult?
choices: Housing in regional areas has become too expensive for young families.
Regional towns have stopped offering support to newcomers.
Internet access in rural areas is still unreliable.
Many companies now require some days in the office.
items.explanation: He says 多くの企業が週に何日かは出社を求めるようになりました. Housing prices, support programs and internet access are not mentioned.

items.stem: How does Mr. Ono respond when the anchor suggests remote work's effect was limited?
choices: He avoids the question and changes the subject.
He politely disagrees and offers another way of reading the data.
He angrily rejects the question as unfair.
He fully agrees, calling remote work a passing fad that has already ended.
items.explanation: He begins いえ、私はそうは考えていません, concedes that the relocation numbers may be disappointing, and then points to dual residence. That is a courteous disagreement with evidence, not agreement, evasion, or anger.

items.stem: In this context, what does 伸び悩んでいます mean?
choices: has fallen sharply
has become impossible to measure
has not grown as much as hoped
has grown rapidly
items.explanation: 伸び悩む means growth has stalled or stayed sluggish. The anchor contrasts it with the earlier spread of remote work, and Ono calls the numbers 期待外れ (disappointing), not a sharp fall or rapid growth. Measurement is not the issue.

items.stem: According to Ms. Takahashi, why do attackers target hospitals?
choices: Hospitals keep large amounts of cash on site.
They expect hospitals to pay quickly because care stops without their systems.
Attackers want to steal new medical technology.
Hospital systems are newer than most, so attackers find them easier to break into.
items.explanation: She says hospitals cannot treat patients without electronic records, so attackers assume a hospital eager to recover will pay. Cash on site and technology theft are not mentioned, and she actually describes hospital equipment as old, not new.

items.stem: What makes countermeasures difficult for hospitals?
choices: Hospitals are not allowed to hire outside experts.
Laws prevent hospitals from keeping backups of patient data outside the hospital.
Too few IT staff and many old devices from different makers.
Doctors refuse to use electronic records.
items.explanation: She cites only one or two system staff and a network of old devices from different manufacturers that is hard to get an overview of. Doctors' attitudes, legal limits on backups and outside experts are not mentioned; she recommends backups.

items.stem: What is her main advice?
choices: Plan on being attacked and prepare to recover fast, starting with offline backups.
Stop using electronic medical records.
Build a defense strong enough that attacks never succeed, so no recovery plan is needed.
Pay attackers quickly to keep downtime short.
items.explanation: She says there is no perfect defense, so hospitals should plan on being attacked (攻撃を受ける前提) and focus on quick recovery, beginning with backups kept off the network. Paying attackers is how attackers expect hospitals to act, not her advice, and she never suggests abandoning electronic records.

items.stem: What is the main issue discussed?
choices: The city wants the exercise cancelled because the convoy is far too large.
The base asks the city to close the Chuo line to all other traffic while the convoy passes.
Parents have demanded that the school change its start time for the convoy.
The convoy's timing clashes with the school commute, so alternatives are explored.
items.explanation: The city says the plan 「登校時間とちょうど重なります」 and it is 「お受けしにくい」, after which a prefectural-road route and traffic guides are proposed. Cancellation, road closure and changing school hours are never raised.

items.stem: Why does the liaison officer say he cannot answer at once about changing the departure time?
choices: He believes the change is unnecessary if guides are posted at crossings.
The U.S. side must first approve any change to the convoy's timing.
It would affect the whole exercise schedule, which is beyond his authority.
He needs to hear directly from the parents before making a decision.
items.explanation: He says 「演習全体の日程に影響が出るので、私の判断ではすぐにはお答えできません」. He does not dismiss the concern, the U.S. side is not mentioned, and it is the city, not he, who will talk to parents.

items.stem: What does the city ask for at the end?
choices: A written apology to the parents of the elementary school
A reply by next Friday so parents can be informed early
Guides posted at every intersection whatever route is used
A new plan in which departure is moved to after 8:30
items.explanation: The city says 「保護者への説明は早めにしたいので、来週の金曜日までにお返事を」. No apology is sought; guides are the base's fallback idea for the Chuo line only; and moving departure later is not requested — the base even mentions leaving earlier.

items.stem: Why does the commander say the open-base tours are not enough?
choices: Attendance was too low to make any difference to how residents view the base.
Those who come are mostly already interested, not the people he most needs to hear.
The tours raised new noise complaints from people who saw the helicopters up close.
Visitors were not allowed into the areas where the training actually takes place.
items.explanation: He notes 「見学に来てくださるのは、もともと自衛隊に関心のある方が多い」 and 「本当に声を聞くべきなのは、来てくださらない方々」. Attendance (about 2,000) is not called low, and no new complaints or access limits are mentioned.

items.stem: What is his position on residents' requests?
choices: He cannot meet them all, but does what he can and explains the rest.
He has changed the training to meet every request raised at meetings.
He treats complaint statistics as the only fair measure of the burden.
He considers the requests secondary, as training needs always come first.
items.explanation: He says 「すべてにお応えできるわけではありません」 yet has reviewed flight routes and feels 「なぜできないのかを説明する責任がある」. He does not meet every request, he says the baby story carried weight 「数字…とは違う」, and he does not dismiss the requests.

items.stem: What is the commentator's main argument?
choices: Screening should be made stricter to stop abuse of the system.
Accepting more refugees and building support for them must go forward together.
Acceptance should be postponed until local support systems are fully ready to receive people.
Local governments and volunteers are best placed to handle all support.
items.explanation: He concludes that numbers and support should advance together like two wheels of a cart. He grants that abuse must be detected but worries screening is already too strict; he calls indefinite postponement a way of dodging international responsibility; and he criticizes leaving support to local governments and volunteers.

items.stem: How does the commentator treat concerns about public safety and social cohesion?
choices: He calls them groundless prejudice.
They deserve a hearing, but isolating newcomers would make them likelier to come true.
He says the government has already resolved them.
He agrees that they are serious enough to justify reducing the number of refugees accepted.
items.explanation: He says rejecting these worries out of hand is not constructive, then argues that isolating refugees could turn the fears into reality, so integration support is needed. He neither dismisses the concerns as prejudice nor uses them to argue for fewer refugees, and he does not claim the government has solved them.

items.stem: In this commentary, 門前払いにする most nearly means
choices: to accept someone on a temporary basis
to put someone's application on hold for a long time
to send someone on to a third country
to turn someone away without real consideration
items.explanation: 門前払い literally means turning a visitor away at the gate, i.e. refusing without proper hearing. He worries strictness is shutting out people who genuinely need protection. Temporary acceptance, transfer to another country and suspension are different outcomes that are not described.

items.stem: The expression 形だけの人道主義 shows the speaker's
choices: approval of leaving support to volunteers
criticism of humanitarianism that exists in name only
worry that humanitarian aid costs too much
praise for a simple, practical approach
items.explanation: 形だけ means 'in form only'. He uses it for a policy that raises numbers but leaves support to others, which he clearly disapproves of. It is neither praise nor a cost argument, and it is exactly the volunteer-dependent approach he is criticizing.

items.stem: What is the commentator's main argument?
choices: The policy makes financial sense but must protect vulnerable residents and involve them.
Every existing settlement should be preserved regardless of cost.
Elderly residents should be required to move to city centers.
Compact-city policies should be abandoned because they waste money and force elderly people to move.
items.explanation: She calls the policy reasonable for cutting costs, warns it can harm elderly suburban residents, and calls for choice and dialogue with residents. She never calls for abandoning it or calls it wasteful, she labels preserving everything irresponsible, and she explicitly rejects forcing people to move.

items.stem: Who does she say is most often left behind in the suburbs?
choices: Owners of small local shops.
Young families who cannot afford housing downtown.
Farmers who must live near their fields.
Elderly people who can no longer drive easily.
items.explanation: 郊外に取り残されるのは、多くの場合、車の運転が難しくなった高齢者です. Young families, farmers and shop owners are not mentioned as the group left behind; closing shops are mentioned only as a cause of inconvenience.

items.stem: Why does she suggest the policy may contradict its own purpose?
choices: It could end up threatening the people who most need support.
It drives people out of the city altogether.
It was designed only to benefit commercial developers.
It raises infrastructure costs for the city instead of lowering them as promised.
items.explanation: She says that if the pursuit of efficiency threatens the lives of those most in need of support, it clashes with the policy's aim. She accepts that it lowers infrastructure costs, and neither emigration from the city nor developer interests are raised.

items.stem: How does she regard the demand that every settlement be kept exactly as it is?
choices: As a reasonable long-term goal.
As irresponsible, given the fiscal reality.
As the most humane option available.
As something residents have never asked for.
items.explanation: She says it is 財政の現実を考えれば無責任な主張. That is plainly critical, so it is not called humane or reasonable, and she says nothing about whether residents have demanded it.

items.stem: What is Okada's central criticism?
choices: The government is relying too heavily on tax increases rather than on bonds.
The amount was set before the threats and funding were explained.
Opposition parties are ignoring the security situation.
Defense spending should not be increased at all.
items.explanation: He says the order is backwards: the figure came first and the content and funding are being debated afterwards. He accepts the need for stronger deterrence, does not claim the government favors taxes, and notes that the security concern is shared across ruling and opposition parties.

items.stem: When Okada calls the process 本末転倒, he means that
choices: the debate ended too quickly
the costs have been underestimated
what should come first has been put last
the plan is likely to be reversed by a future government
items.explanation: 本末転倒 means confusing the essential with the secondary, getting priorities backwards. It directly follows his remark that the order is reversed (順番が逆). It says nothing about future reversal, cost estimates, or the length of the debate, which in fact has not ended.

items.stem: Why does Nakamura say the government is in a 痛し痒し position?
choices: Either funding option hurts someone: households now, or future generations later.
The government cannot decide whether defense spending is needed.
Bond markets have refused to buy government debt.
Allies want more spending, but the public opposes any increase and the budget is already tight.
items.explanation: 痛し痒し describes a choice where every option has a downside. Bonds shift the burden to children; tax rises burden households already hit by inflation. The need for spending is not in doubt, allies are not mentioned, and there is no bond-market refusal.

items.stem: Which best describes Okada's stance on strengthening deterrence?
choices: He opposes it on principle.
He accepts the need for it but is critical of how the decision was made.
He considers it irrelevant, since the security situation has not really changed.
He fully supports the government's handling of it.
items.explanation: He says 抑止力を高める必要性自体は、私も認めます, while criticizing the order of decisions and demanding accountability. That rules out principled opposition and full support, and he explicitly agrees the security environment is becoming harsher, so he does not think nothing has changed.

items.stem: What is the core disagreement between the two speakers?
choices: Whether cyberattacks on infrastructure are a real threat.
Whether private companies, not the state, should be responsible for defending their own networks.
Whether the Self-Defense Forces should have a cyber unit at all.
How to balance proactive cyber defense against protecting the secrecy of communications.
items.explanation: Ishida argues active defense is unavoidable; Morikawa fears vague limits on analyzing communications could hollow out constitutional secrecy of communications. Morikawa explicitly agrees the threat is real, and neither SDF cyber units nor private-sector responsibility is discussed.

items.stem: Why does Morikawa say Ishida's explanation 腑に落ちない?
choices: She does not understand the technical terms he uses.
She believes the government is already secretly reading private e-mail on a large scale.
She thinks the cyber threat is exaggerated.
Unless the law sets clear limits and oversight, the limits could be stretched.
items.explanation: 腑に落ちない means 'not convinced'. She asks who stores what, for how long, and how far an independent body's authority reaches, warning that 限られる can be interpreted ever more broadly unless defined by law. She makes no claim that e-mail is being read now, shows no confusion over terms, and accepts that the threat is real.

items.stem: On what point does Ishida agree with Morikawa?
choices: Procedures should be made as strict as possible.
Rules should be settled after an emergency arises.
The content of communications should be analyzed.
Some oversight mechanism is needed.
items.explanation: He says 監視の仕組みが必要だという点は、私も同意します. He insists content will not be analyzed, warns against making procedures too heavy, and it is Morikawa who argues rules must be set in peacetime, not after an emergency.

items.stem: What is the point of Morikawa's final remark?
choices: To suggest abandoning active cyber defense altogether.
To propose postponing the debate until an emergency.
To argue that the rules must be set in calm times rather than during a crisis.
To concede that speed matters more than rules.
items.explanation: She answers Ishida's worry about slow procedures by saying that is exactly why rules should be fixed in peacetime, since calm judgment is impossible in an emergency. She concedes nothing, argues against waiting for an emergency, and never calls for abandoning the policy.

items.stem: What is the main subject of the discussion?
choices: Whether a mayoral candidate really received illegal donations before the election.
Why the correction was published before the vote.
How generative AI can be used to make campaign videos.
How society should respond to fake content that can sway elections.
items.explanation: The speakers use a fake video in a mayoral race as a starting point to debate platform removal duties versus free speech and media literacy. The video was fake, so the donation claim is not the issue; AI is discussed as a threat, not a campaign tool; and the correction came after the vote.

items.stem: Why is Kawakami wary of requiring platforms to delete posts more aggressively?
choices: Most fake videos are harmless jokes.
Deletion would be too costly for small companies.
Such powers could be misused to silence inconvenient speech.
Platforms lack the technology to detect fake videos.
items.explanation: He warns that a system in which companies or the government decide what is false could become a tool for suppressing inconvenient speech, and raises the balance with freedom of expression. He does not claim detection is impossible for platforms, mentions no costs, and treats fake videos as a real problem.

items.stem: As Kawakami uses it, いたちごっこ refers to
choices: a decisive win for detection technology
a cooperation agreement between the companies that make and detect videos
a children's game used to teach media literacy
an endless cycle in which each side keeps catching up with the other
items.explanation: いたちごっこ describes a cat-and-mouse contest with no end. He uses it for fake-video makers and detectors each advancing, which is why there is no decisive solution. It is not a literal game, a victory, or an agreement.

items.stem: Which best describes Kawakami's final position?
choices: Stronger deletion rules are the fastest and best solution.
The problem cannot be solved and should be ignored.
Detection technology will soon end the problem.
Building people's ability to check sources is slow but the most reliable path.
items.explanation: He calls education in checking information sources a detour that is actually the shortest route, admitting it takes time, and says there is no other royal road for protecting democracy. He does not give up, he is cautious about deletion rules, and he says detection has no decisive answer.

items.stem: What is Sugiyama's main view of the current state of the alliance?
choices: Airing disagreements publicly has made the alliance stronger.
The alliance has never had internal disagreements.
Disagreements are nothing new; what has changed is that they are now aired in public.
The alliance is facing an unprecedented collapse because its members no longer share interests.
items.explanation: He says the alliance was never monolithic and interests always clashed; the difference now is that disagreements are spoken of openly. He does not describe a collapse, he says disagreements always existed, and he argues public airing makes compromise harder, not the alliance stronger.

items.stem: When Sugiyama says the alliance was never 一枚岩, he means it was never
choices: based on a written treaty
open to new members
completely united inside
officially recognized by both governments
items.explanation: 一枚岩 ('a single slab of rock') means perfectly united. He immediately explains that even when the allies look in step from outside, interests always collide inside. Recognition, treaties and membership are not what the idiom refers to.

items.stem: Why does he think making negotiations fully public can backfire?
choices: Reporters often get the details wrong.
Foreign intelligence services can use the published details to learn negotiating positions.
Each side must look tough at home, which makes compromise harder.
The public loses interest in foreign policy.
items.explanation: He says full disclosure forces both sides to show a strong stance at home (国内向けに強い姿勢), so meeting halfway becomes harder. Espionage, public interest and inaccurate reporting are not mentioned.

items.stem: How does Sugiyama characterize his advice to young diplomats?
choices: As commonplace-sounding, yet in the end the essence of the job.
As a secret he has never shared before.
As something he learned only after retiring.
As outdated in today's world.
items.explanation: He calls it 月並み (commonplace) but says it all comes down to this (これに尽きる). He does not present it as a secret, as a late lesson, or as outdated.

items.stem: What does the spokesperson's answer about the plan's status imply?
choices: The extension has been withdrawn because of the city's angry reaction to the leak.
The city has already given its formal consent, so only the start date is undecided.
Everything, including whether to extend at all, now depends entirely on the city's consent.
The extension itself is effectively set; only details like days and period are open.
items.explanation: He says 「訓練の必要性そのものは変わりません」 while days and period will be set 「市のご意見を伺いながら」, and he accepts the reporter's summary that the extension is 「譲れない」. Nothing is withdrawn, the city has not agreed, and the extension itself is not put up for consent.

items.stem: What does 「地元のご理解なしに訓練を続けることが、現実的には難しい」 suggest?
choices: The base will suspend all night flights until the city has formally agreed to the new schedule.
The base views local opposition as irrelevant and intends to proceed regardless.
Although consent is not formally required, the base knows it needs local acceptance.
The base holds the press responsible for having damaged local understanding.
items.explanation: 「現実的には」 contrasts practical reality with the formal position that the extension is not up for veto: the base admits it cannot operate against local feeling. No suspension is promised, opposition is not dismissed, and the leak is treated as the base's own information-management failure (「情報の管理に不十分な点があった」).

items.stem: How does the spokesperson handle the final question?
choices: He admits that the extension would be dropped in that case.
He warns that the training would go ahead in any case.
He declines to speculate and restates the aim of explaining fully.
He refers the reporter to the city for an answer to that.
items.explanation: He answers 「仮定のご質問にはお答えを控えさせていただきます」 and turns to 「説明を尽くすことに全力を挙げたい」. He commits neither to dropping nor to forcing the plan, and does not redirect the question to the city.

items.stem: What is Professor Kawabata's main argument?
choices: Training and residents' lives cannot be reconciled, so one must take priority.
The burden falls unevenly, so residents need a real voice, not money or a veto.
Grants to local towns already balance the burden, so no further step is needed.
Residents should be given a veto over training plans that affect their area.
items.explanation: He says the core is 「負担の偏りをどう扱うか」, that money 「には限界があります」, and that one should separate 「同意と拒否権」 — no veto, but a real hearing before decisions. He rejects the either/or framing and the view that grants settle the matter.

items.stem: How does he assess the grants paid to local governments?
choices: They do real good, but cannot replace residents' sense of being heard.
They are wasted, since they are rarely spent on residents' actual needs.
They are sufficient, since they pay for soundproofing and public works.
They are harmful, since they make residents more dependent on the base.
items.explanation: He grants that 「交付金には一定の意味があります」 as they fund soundproofing, then says what residents seek is 「自分たちの声が決定に届いているという実感」. He neither calls them wasted or sufficient, nor talks about dependence.

items.stem: What does 「何も変わらない話し合いに、人は二度目は来ませんから」 imply?
choices: Residents are basically uninterested in meetings about training schedules.
Briefings should be held only once, so as to avoid wasting the residents' valuable time.
The base should stop holding briefings and communicate only in writing.
Consultation keeps its credibility only if it can actually change some outcomes.
items.explanation: It follows his warning that 「形だけの説明会を重ねれば、かえって不信を深める」 and his call to leave room where input 「実際に変わりうる」. People stop coming because nothing changes, not because they are uninterested; he wants better consultation, not fewer or written-only briefings.
